title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
description: Find the leftmost and rightmost index of a target in a sorted array using two binary searches.

data.text: Given a sorted array of integers `nums` and a target value, find the starting and ending position of the target. If the target is not found, return `[-1, -1]`. You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.

Run binary search twice: once modified to always move right on a match (`left = mid + 1`) to find the leftmost index, and once to always move left on a match (`right = mid - 1`) to find the rightmost. Each search is `O(log n)`, so the total is `O(log n)` time and `O(1)` space.

data.title: Lower and upper bound O(log n)

data.text: Most standard libraries expose `lower_bound` (first index ≥ target) and `upper_bound` (first index > target). The first position is `lower_bound(target)`; the last is `upper_bound(target) - 1`. Validate both point at the target. C# has no built-in, but the two helpers above are exactly this.

data.title: Lower/upper bound idea

data.caption: Finding the leftmost index always moves right past a match; the rightmost search moves left past a match. Both converge in O(log n).

graph TB
    A[left=0 right=5 target=8] --> B[mid=2 nums[2]=7 < 8]
    B --> C[left=3 right=5]
    C --> D[mid=4 nums[4]=8 match]
    D --> E[findFirst: right=3 to go left]
    D --> F[findLast: left=5 to go right]

    F --> H[converges at index 4 = last]

data.title: What improved?
data.text: A naive linear scan finds the target but then walks outward to find the boundaries — O(n). By encoding 'keep going left' vs 'keep going right' into the binary search's match branch, both bounds are found in logarithmic time.
